newsitem.title: CHINA: China fibre industry hit by low priced imports.
newsitem.headline: China fibre industry hit by low priced imports.

text.p: China's chemical fibre industry is threatened by cut-price imported products which are squeezing the profits of many domestic producers, industry analysts said on Friday.

"Imported chemical fibre products are greatly hurting the domestic market," said an official with the state-owned Shanghai Chemical Fibre (Group) Co. "They are being sold at prices nearly equal to our raw materials prices."
The official said the group runs 22 major chemical fibre producers in Shanghai, of which half are suffering losses.

China's leading chemical fibre maker, Shanghai Lianhua Fibre Co on Friday reported a tiny net profit of 28,500 yuan ($3,434) for 1996 compared with 9.508 million yuan in 1995, based on international accounting standards.

"Since the second half of 1995, China's chemical fibre industry has been hit by big changes in the market," Lianhua's annual report said. "Prices of chemical fibre products have been falling sharply with firms in the industry making little or no profit."
The price of filaments, a key chemical fibre product, has declined almost 20 percent over the past year, figures from industry analysts showed. They are expected to fall further this year.

According to figures released by an official with the China Chemical Fibre Industrial Association (CCFIA), China imported 1.6 million tonnes of chemical fibre in 1996 compared with around 1.3 million tonnes in 1995.
China's total output of chemical fibre was 3.34 million tonnes in 1996, he said.

Sources involved in the industry said tolling, the payment of tariffs on goods imported for processing and re-export, was being evaded by many companies which were actually selling the product on the domestic market.
"By tax evasion, these companies can sell their products at much lower prices on the domestic market, which constitutes a big threat to local producers," an industrial analyst said.
China's tariffs on finished chemical fibre goods are over 10 percent and value-added taxes total another 17 percent, a CCFIA official said.
"In this way, foreign companies can sell their products as much as 2,000-yuan per tonne lower than domestic manufacturers," he said.
Local producers said they have appealed to the government to introduce regulations to protect their interests, otherwise the industry will have difficulty recovering in the near-term.
"We have no way to deal with the situation," said the official with the Shanghai Chemical Fibre (Group) Co. "It depends on the government to work out some policies to solve the problem."
The CCFIA official said they were trying to work out suitable measures, but declined to elaborate.
Industrial analysts said the chemical fibre market would remain weak for at least the next two years given the overall over-supply in the Southeast Asian region.

"Many factories planned several years ago have now begun operations, resulting in heavy over-supply and severe competition," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage. "The balance between supply and demand will not be achieved until at least 1999." ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
